title: Ownership and Moves
intro: This is the big one. Every value in Rust has exactly one owner. When the owner goes away, the value is freed. Assigning a value to another variable moves it: the new variable becomes the owner, and the old one can't be used.

coming_from.go: In Go, `b := a` makes two slices share one array. In Rust, `let b = a;` moves the `Vec` to `b` and `a` can't be used any more, so if you want two you write `a.clone()`.
coming_from.kotlin: In Kotlin, `val b = a` gives two names for one list. In Rust it moves the list to `b`, `a` is no longer usable, and the list is freed when `b` goes out of scope instead of by a garbage collector.
coming_from.python: In Python, `b = a` gives two names for one list. In Rust it moves the list, `a` can't be used again, and `a.clone()` is how you get a real second copy.
coming_from.typescript: In TypeScript, `const b = a` makes two references to one array. In Rust it moves the array to `b`, `a` can't be used any more, and the memory is freed when `b` goes out of scope, with no garbage collector.
coming_from.java: Java lets two variables share one object, and the garbage collector frees it later. In Rust `let b = a;` moves the `Vec` to `b`, and `a` can't be used again; the value is freed when `b` goes out of scope, with no GC.
coming_from.csharp: In C#, `var b = a;` gives two references to one `List`. In Rust it moves the value, so `a` is no longer usable, and the memory is freed the moment its single owner goes out of scope instead of by a garbage collector.
coming_from.c: Ownership is your "who calls `free`" rule, written into the types. After `let b = a;` the compiler forbids touching `a`, so a double free or a use after free can't compile.
coming_from.cpp: `let b = a;` is `auto b = std::move(a);`, not `auto b = a;`: nothing is copied. And the compiler checks the move: using `a` afterwards is a compile error, not a read of a moved-from object. No destructor runs on the moved-from `a` either.

notes: A move does not copy the list. It copies the 24-byte header (pointer, length, capacity) and marks the old name as unusable. Moving a huge Vec is just as cheap as moving a tiny one.

Some types are copied instead of moved: numbers, bool, char, shared references `&T`, and tuples and arrays of those. They're called `Copy`. A plain copy of their bytes gives a complete, independent value, and there is nothing to free.
Why bother? Rust has no garbage collector. "Exactly one owner" is how it knows when to free memory, and that it frees it exactly once.

gotcha.title: Using a variable after assigning it to another
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, `b := a` and then printing both is perfectly fine. They share one array.
gotcha.rust_sees: After `let b = a`, `b` owns the list. `a` is a name with nothing behind it.
gotcha.why: Rust has no garbage collector, so it frees the list when its owner goes away. That only works if there is exactly one owner. With two, C would free the list twice (see the C version), and a garbage-collected language gives you two names for one list, so a change through `b` shows up in `a`. Rust's rule is one owner, and assignment hands it over. If you only want to look at the list through a second name, borrow it with `&`. That is the next lesson. The compiler's `help:` suggests `a.clone()`, which makes a second list; borrowing costs nothing.

go.says: Go runs this and prints [1 2 3] twice. `a` and `b` share one array, so a change through `b` would show up in `a` too.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints [1, 2, 3] twice. `a` and `b` are the same list, so a change through `b` would show up in `a` too.

python.says: Python prints the list twice. `b = a` doesn't copy or move anything: both names point to the same list, so a change through `b` would show up in `a` too.

typescript.says: Prints the array twice. `a` and `b` are two names for the same array, so a change through `b` would show up in `a` too.

java.says: Both names point at the same list, so it prints twice. A change through `b` would show up in `a` too, as the lesson program shows.

csharp.says: Both lines print [1, 2, 3] because a and b are the same list. A change made through b would show up in a too.

c.says: C copies the pointer, so `a` and `b` share one buffer and both get freed. gcc builds it without a warning, and AddressSanitizer reports the double free.

cpp.says: `auto b = a;` copies the whole vector, so it prints [1, 2, 3] twice. That's correct, but it allocates a second buffer. `auto b = std::move(a);` is what Rust's `let b = a;` does. It leaves `a` empty, but nothing stops you from reading `a` afterwards. clang-tidy's `bugprone-use-after-move` check catches many of those reads, but a lint isn't a guarantee.

go.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a := []int{1, 2, 3}
	b := a         // a and b now share the SAME array
	b[0] = 100     // change through b...
	fmt.Println(a) // ...and a changed too: [100 2 3]
	fmt.Println(b)

	x := 5
	y := x
	fmt.Println(x, y)
}

kotlin.code:
fun main() {
    val a = mutableListOf(1, 2, 3)
    val b = a        // a and b point at the SAME list
    b[0] = 100
    println(a)       // [100, 2, 3]
    println(b)

    val x = 5
    val y = x
    println("$x $y")
}
